subject: Hospitality
title: Tipping Culture Around the World
description: A micro-lesson that makes Tipping Culture Around the World usable.

hook.text: Americans tip 15–20%. Japanese find tipping insulting. Australians include service in the price. Tipping has no global rule.

buildup.text: In the U.S., tips evolved because restaurant owners wanted to pay workers less. Tips shifted labor costs to customers.

discovery.text: Research shows tipping correlates more with server appearance and friendliness than with food quality or service speed.

twist.text: Studies also show racial bias in tipping. Servers of color consistently receive lower tips for identical service quality.

climax.text: The 'no-tipping' movement tries to replace tips with fair wages. But cultural habits are proving incredibly hard to change.

punchline.text: A system born from inequality, sustained by habit. Tipping is complicated.

quiz.question: Why is tipping considered insulting in Japan?
options: Good service is expected as standard—tipping implies it's not
